demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with the more trauma-disconnected pattern implied by emotionless/numb recall and sensory reliving. Those can occasionally coexist, but this combination is clinically questionable as a compact 3-item profile because one item suggests relatively integrated verbal access while the others suggest poorly integrated or detached trauma memory.

issues.item: Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' is a poor fit for the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. It implies an intruder/home-security threat that is not supported by the other selected Memory or Negative Appraisal items, which center more on guilt, identity change, and trauma recall rather than fear of break-in or assault. This makes the Threat profile less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, repeated checking of doors and windows being locked suggests a home-intrusion/interpersonal danger theme that is not supported by the other threat, memory, or appraisal items. The rest of the profile centers on guilt, altered self-view, disconnection, and poorly elaborated trauma memory rather than fear of external attack.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Loss of connection to community and culture is not impossible, but in this profile it is insufficiently linked to the stated trauma and the other selected items. The other appraisals focus on self-doubt and identity change after causing harm, whereas this item introduces a broader sociocultural rupture that is not reflected elsewhere in memory or threat content, making the node less coherent.

vignette:
Nadia, a 31-year-old social media manager, still feels the jolt of the steering wheel in her hands when she thinks about that rainy Tuesday. She had been driving home after a long day of managing campaign posts, glanced at her phone for a split second to approve a sponsored story, and never saw the cyclist until the thud. The man survived but with a shattered femur and a permanent limp. No charges were filed, but Nadia carries something heavier than legal guilt: she has come to believe she cannot trust herself to do the right thing, that the person she used to be—confident, reliable—has become unrecognisable, and that she has permanently changed for the worse. These negative appraisals have taken root so deeply that they now colour every moment of her daily life, making her feel as if danger is lurking at all times. At her desk, when a colleague taps her shoulder to ask a question, she reacts with an exaggerated startle, her heart hammering as though she has just been attacked. She knows intellectually that nothing is wrong, but her body insists otherwise, flooding her with fear and shame—false alarms that only reinforce her sense that she is fundamentally broken.

The memory of the accident intrudes in strange, visceral ways. Sometimes when she is putting on her jacket, she catches a phantom whiff of wet asphalt and copper, the olfactory recall so vivid that she freezes mid-step and the scene unfolds in her mind against her will. Other times, when she tries to describe what happened to a friend or a therapist, she finds herself unable to find the right words—the details feel locked away, and she recites the event in a flat, detached voice, as if it happened to a stranger. This emotionless recall disturbs her even more than the flashbacks, because it confirms her worst suspicion: she is no longer the same person. Her negative appraisals about permanent damage feed directly into these memory problems: when she cannot feel the pain anymore, she interprets it as proof that something in her has died. 

The causal loops tighten without her noticing. Every time she startles at an unexpected touch—at work, a colleague brushing past her in the hallway—the adrenaline surge drags the memory of the accident back into her consciousness, the smell of rain and the sound of the impact playing on repeat. And each time that memory surfaces, it strips away another layer of her old self, reinforcing the thought, “I’m permanently damaged.” She has started to avoid physical contact altogether, pulling away from hugs, sitting at the far end of the conference table so no one can accidentally graze her. One concrete consequence is that her professional relationships have suffered: her team now finds her cold and distant, and she was passed over for a promotion because her manager noted she seemed “unapproachable.” Nadia knows she has changed, and that knowledge makes her feel even more unsafe—a cycle that has spiralled over the six months since the accident. 

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last week when she was editing a client’s social media calendar and saw a post about cycling safety. The combination of the onscreen image and the unexpected ping of a notification caused such a violent startle that she knocked her coffee across her keyboard, burst into tears, and sat trembling for twenty minutes. She realised she could not keep pretending the wreckage was contained to that rainy afternoon. Now, sitting in the waiting room, she is terrified that therapy will only confirm what she already fears: that she is irreparably different. But a smaller, quieter part of her hopes that maybe, just maybe, she might find a way to trust herself again.
